symptoms.sourceText: Cramping, spasmodic lower abdominal or suprapubic pain occurring with menstruation, typically beginning a few hours before or with the onset of bleeding and lasting 24-72 hours
Pain radiating to the lower back and inner thighs

In secondary dysmenorrhoea the pain starts earlier in the cycle, lasts longer, may persist after bleeding stops, and is often accompanied by deep dyspareunia, heavy or irregular bleeding, chronic pelvic pain, subfertility, and dyschezia
Emotional symptoms such as depression and anxiety may also occur

signs: Inspect the vulva for erythema, oedema, excoriation, fissuring, satellite lesions (candidiasis), ulcers or warts. SPECULUM examination to assess the discharge and the cervix and to take swabs. BACTERIAL VAGINOSIS: thin, homogeneous, grey-white discharge coating the vaginal walls, vaginal pH above 4.5, a positive amine (whiff) test on adding 10% KOH, and clue cells on saline wet mount (Amsel criteria). CANDIDIASIS: thick, white, adherent curdy plaques with underlying erythema, normal pH of 4.0-4.5, and budding yeasts and pseudohyphae on KOH mount. TRICHOMONIASIS: profuse frothy yellow-green discharge, pH above 4.5, a punctate haemorrhagic 'strawberry' cervix, and motile flagellated trophozoites on saline wet mount. CERVICITIS: mucopurulent endocervical discharge with a friable cervix that bleeds on contact - take NAAT swabs for Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae. BIMANUAL examination for cervical motion tenderness, uterine and adnexal tenderness or masses (pelvic inflammatory disease)

symptoms.sourceText: Central or retrosternal chest discomfort described as heaviness, tightness, pressure, squeezing or a band-like constriction rather than sharp pain, precipitated by exertion or emotional stress and relieved within minutes by rest or sublingual nitrate

Breathlessness on exertion (an anginal equivalent, especially in the elderly, women and diabetics)
Symptoms worse in cold weather, after heavy meals or when walking uphill
The Levine sign (a clenched fist held over the sternum)
Risk factors - age, male sex, smoking, diabetes, hypertension, dyslipidaemia, obesity, sedentary lifestyle and a family history of premature coronary disease
Atypical symptoms such as sharp fleeting chest pain or prolonged dull ache, particularly in women and diabetics

signs: Physical examination is frequently NORMAL between attacks, and a normal examination never excludes the diagnosis. During an episode there may be tachycardia, a rise in blood pressure, a fourth heart sound, a transient apical systolic murmur of ischaemic mitral regurgitation, and basal crackles. Look for evidence of atherosclerosis and risk factors - arcus senilis and xanthelasma, tendon xanthomata, carotid and femoral bruits, reduced peripheral pulses, hypertension, central obesity and diabetic changes on fundoscopy

anaemia, thyrotoxicosis and aortic stenosis (a slow-rising pulse with an ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotids) can precipitate or mimic angina. A RESTING ECG is normal in about half of patients but may show ST depression, T-wave inversion, pathological Q waves from prior infarction or left ventricular hypertrophy. Confirm with exercise ECG (ST depression of 1 mm or more that is horizontal or downsloping), stress echocardiography, myocardial perfusion imaging or CT coronary angiography, with invasive coronary angiography where revascularisation is contemplated. Grade severity by the Canadian Cardiovascular Society classification I to IV
Physical examination often normal, but look for evidence of atherosclerotic disease (e.g., diminished arterial pulses, bruits).

signs: The patient is typically anxious, restless, pale, sweating and cool peripherally. Tachycardia (or BRADYCARDIA and hypotension in inferior/right ventricular infarction with vagal activation)
blood pressure may be raised, normal or low
low-grade fever after 12-24 hours
a fourth heart sound is almost always present, a third heart sound indicates significant left ventricular dysfunction

a new apical pansystolic murmur suggests ischaemic MITRAL REGURGITATION from papillary muscle dysfunction or rupture, and a new harsh pansystolic murmur with a thrill suggests VENTRICULAR SEPTAL RUPTURE

TIME IS MYOCARDIUM. Danger signs requiring the highest level of care: cardiogenic shock with hypotension, oliguria, cold clammy peripheries and confusion
acute pulmonary oedema

right ventricular infarction with hypotension and clear lungs (nitrates and diuretics are DANGEROUS - give fluids)
recurrent or ongoing chest pain after treatment
mechanical complications
stroke. DO NOT give nitrates if the systolic BP is below 90 mmHg, in right ventricular infarction, or within 24-48 hours of phosphodiesterase inhibitor use

symptoms.sourceText: Palpitations - an awareness of the heartbeat, described as racing, pounding, fluttering, skipping, thumping or irregular
Anxiety and a sense of panic
symptoms.masterName: Anxiety and a sense of panic

symptoms.sourceText: Neck pulsation (cannon A waves in AV dissociation, and the 'frog sign' in AV nodal re-entrant tachycardia)
Polyuria after an episode of supraventricular tachycardia
Sudden onset and sudden termination suggesting a re-entrant tachycardia, in contrast to the gradual onset and offset of sinus tachycardia
Termination by Valsalva or carotid sinus massage
Precipitants - caffeine, alcohol, nicotine, stimulant drugs, decongestants, thyroid disease, anaemia, fever, electrolyte disturbance, structural heart disease and stress
A family history of sudden cardiac death before the age of 40 is a critical historical point

signs: Assess the pulse rate, rhythm, volume and character
an IRREGULARLY IRREGULAR pulse with a pulse deficit (apex rate exceeding radial rate) indicates ATRIAL FIBRILLATION
a regular rapid pulse of 150/min suggests atrial flutter with 2:1 block
cannon A waves in the jugular venous pulse indicate atrioventricular dissociation (ventricular tachycardia or complete heart block)

variable intensity of the first heart sound also indicates AV dissociation. Assess haemodynamic stability - blood pressure, level of consciousness, peripheral perfusion, chest pain and signs of heart failure. Examine for underlying causes: thyrotoxicosis (goitre, tremor, lid lag), valvular disease (especially mitral stenosis in atrial fibrillation), heart failure, anaemia and alcohol excess. THE 12-LEAD ECG DURING SYMPTOMS IS THE DEFINITIVE INVESTIGATION - assess rate, regularity, P-wave presence and relationship to QRS, and QRS width: narrow-complex regular (sinus tachycardia, atrial flutter, AVNRT, AVRT), narrow-complex irregular (atrial fibrillation, multifocal atrial tachycardia), broad-complex regular (ventricular tachycardia until proven otherwise, or SVT with aberrancy), broad-complex irregular (atrial fibrillation with bundle branch block or pre-excitation, polymorphic VT/torsades). Look for a delta wave and short PR interval (Wolff-Parkinson-White), a prolonged QTc, Brugada-type ST elevation in V1-V3, epsilon waves, and evidence of prior infarction. Ambulatory Holter or event monitoring for intermittent symptoms
echocardiography for structural disease
check electrolytes (potassium, magnesium, calcium), thyroid function, full blood count and drug levels

redFlags: IMMEDIATE EMERGENCY - any arrhythmia with ADVERSE FEATURES: shock (systolic BP below 90 mmHg, pallor, sweating, cold clammy extremities, confusion), syncope, myocardial ischaemia with chest pain, or acute heart failure - requires urgent synchronised cardioversion or pacing. Also emergency: broad-complex tachycardia (treat as VENTRICULAR TACHYCARDIA)
polymorphic VT/torsades de pointes with a prolonged QT (stop the offending drug, give magnesium)
ventricular fibrillation and cardiac arrest (immediate defibrillation and CPR)
complete heart block or Mobitz type II block with bradycardia and syncope (pacing)

atrial fibrillation with pre-excitation (AVOID AV nodal blocking drugs - digoxin, verapamil, diltiazem and adenosine can precipitate ventricular fibrillation). Refer urgently: syncope during exertion or while supine, or syncope without warning (suggests a malignant arrhythmia)
a family history of sudden cardiac death under 40
new atrial fibrillation (assess CHA2DS2-VASc score for anticoagulation and HAS-BLED for bleeding risk - stroke prevention is the priority)
palpitations with structural heart disease or reduced ejection fraction
documented sustained arrhythmia
digoxin toxicity
severe electrolyte derangement
conditions.firstLine: supportive care - reassurance and removal of aggravating factors (e.g., caffeine or alcohol) may be all that is needed.

symptoms.sourceText: Breathlessness on exertion, orthopnoea and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea
A history of sore throat in childhood followed by migratory joint pains and fever
Cough and haemoptysis (pulmonary venous congestion in mitral stenosis)
Hoarseness from left atrial enlargement compressing the recurrent laryngeal nerve (Ortner syndrome)
Ankle swelling and abdominal distension in right heart failure
Embolic events - stroke or limb ischaemia from left atrial thrombus in atrial fibrillation
Growth retardation and recurrent illness in children

In acute rheumatic fever, a migratory polyarthritis of large joints, fever, involuntary purposeless movements (Sydenham chorea), painless subcutaneous nodules and a serpiginous rash 2-4 weeks after streptococcal pharyngitis
Advanced disease may present with significant heart failure symptoms such as fatigue, orthopnoea, and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea

signs: ACUTE RHEUMATIC FEVER is diagnosed by the REVISED JONES CRITERIA - two major, or one major and two minor manifestations, plus evidence of preceding group A streptococcal infection (raised or rising ASO or anti-DNase B titre, positive throat culture or rapid antigen test). MAJOR: carditis (clinical or subclinical on echocardiography), polyarthritis, Sydenham chorea, erythema marginatum (a pink, non-pruritic, serpiginous macular rash with central clearing on the trunk and proximal limbs, sparing the face), and subcutaneous nodules (firm, painless, mobile, 0.5-2 cm over extensor surfaces and bony prominences). MINOR: fever, arthralgia, raised ESR or CRP, and a prolonged PR interval. CHRONIC RHEUMATIC VALVULAR DISEASE - MITRAL STENOSIS: a tapping, non-displaced apex beat, a loud first heart sound, an opening snap and a low-pitched rumbling mid-diastolic murmur with presystolic accentuation at the apex, best heard in the left lateral position with the bell, a malar flush, atrial fibrillation with an irregularly irregular pulse, a loud P2 and right ventricular heave with pulmonary hypertension. MITRAL REGURGITATION: a displaced hyperdynamic apex, a soft first sound, a third heart sound and a blowing pansystolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla. AORTIC REGURGITATION: a collapsing (water-hammer) pulse, wide pulse pressure, a displaced heaving apex and an early diastolic decrescendo murmur at the left sternal edge on leaning forward in expiration, with an Austin Flint murmur, plus Corrigan's, de Musset's, Quincke's, Traube's and Duroziez's signs. AORTIC STENOSIS: a slow-rising low-volume pulse, narrow pulse pressure, a heaving undisplaced apex and an ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotids with a soft or absent A2. ECHOCARDIOGRAPHY is diagnostic and grades severity
ECG shows P mitrale, atrial fibrillation, LVH or right ventricular hypertrophy
chest radiograph shows left atrial enlargement with a double right heart border, splaying of the carina, a straightened left heart border and pulmonary venous congestion or valve calcification
Heart failure signs including elevated jugular venous pressure, pulmonary crackles, and peripheral edema

redFlags: Acute pulmonary oedema or severe breathlessness at rest
haemoptysis, especially massive
new atrial fibrillation with fast ventricular rate and haemodynamic compromise (anticoagulate - the embolic risk in rheumatic mitral stenosis with AF is very high)
systemic embolism causing stroke or acute limb ischaemia
SYNCOPE, ANGINA OR HEART FAILURE IN SEVERE AORTIC STENOSIS (each carries a poor prognosis and mandates urgent surgical referral)

fever with a new or changing murmur, splinter haemorrhages, Osler nodes, Janeway lesions, Roth spots and splenomegaly (INFECTIVE ENDOCARDITIS - take three sets of blood cultures before antibiotics and arrange echocardiography urgently)
pregnancy in a woman with significant mitral stenosis (high risk of decompensation - needs joint cardiac and obstetric care)
severe valve disease on echocardiography
any acute rheumatic fever (admit, treat the streptococcal infection, and start LONG-TERM SECONDARY PROPHYLAXIS with benzathine penicillin to prevent recurrence and progressive valve damage)
chorea
failure of medical therapy
Exacerbation of heart failure symptoms requiring urgent intervention
referralCriteria: Referral to a cardiologist for patients with severe valvular heart disease or those needing surgical intervention
Referral for echocardiography in suspected cases of severe heart failure symptoms or significant murmur changes
Consideration for joint management with obstetrics in pregnant women with severe mitral stenosis

symptoms.sourceText: Sudden onset of a focal neurological deficit - unilateral weakness or numbness of the face, arm and leg
Difficulty speaking or understanding speech (dysphasia) or slurred speech (dysarthria)
Sudden visual loss or double vision
symptoms.masterName: Sudden visual loss or double vision

symptoms.sourceText: Facial droop with sparing of the forehead (upper motor neuron pattern)
Headache (more typical of haemorrhage but occurs in ischaemia)
Visual field loss or homonymous hemianopia
Vertigo, nausea and vomiting in posterior circulation stroke
Reduced level of consciousness in large strokes
Neglect and denial of deficit in non-dominant hemisphere strokes

Risk factors - hypertension, atrial fibrillation, diabetes, smoking, dyslipidaemia, previous stroke, carotid stenosis and prosthetic valves. the exact time of symptom onset, or the time the patient was last seen well, must be established, as it governs eligibility for thrombolysis
Profound abulia (a delay in verbal and motor response)

signs: Rapid recognition using FAST - Face drooping, Arm weakness, Speech difficulty, Time to call emergency services. Full neurological examination: level of consciousness (Glasgow Coma Scale)
higher functions and language (fluency, comprehension, repetition, naming)
cranial nerves including visual fields, conjugate gaze deviation TOWARDS the side of the lesion in hemispheric stroke, and pupillary responses
UPPER MOTOR NEURON pattern of weakness with initial flaccidity progressing to spasticity, hyperreflexia and an EXTENSOR PLANTAR RESPONSE
sensory loss
cerebellar signs

and gait. Localise the territory - ANTERIOR CEREBRAL ARTERY: contralateral leg-predominant weakness with sensory loss and urinary incontinence. MIDDLE CEREBRAL ARTERY: contralateral face and arm-predominant weakness and sensory loss, homonymous hemianopia, gaze deviation, with dysphasia if the dominant hemisphere is involved and neglect if the non-dominant. POSTERIOR CIRCULATION: vertigo, diplopia, dysarthria, dysphagia, ataxia, crossed sensory findings and cortical blindness. LACUNAR: pure motor, pure sensory, sensorimotor, ataxic hemiparesis or clumsy-hand dysarthria without cortical signs. Score severity with the NIHSS. Check pulse for ATRIAL FIBRILLATION, blood pressure in both arms, carotid bruits, heart murmurs, fundoscopy for hypertensive or embolic changes, and CAPILLARY BLOOD GLUCOSE IMMEDIATELY (hypoglycaemia is the great mimic). URGENT NON-CONTRAST CT BRAIN is required first to exclude haemorrhage
early ischaemic signs include loss of grey-white differentiation, insular ribbon sign, a hyperdense MCA sign and sulcal effacement, while infarct hypodensity may not appear for hours
MRI with diffusion-weighted imaging detects ischaemia within minutes
CT or MR angiography identifies large vessel occlusion

redFlags: STROKE IS A TIME-CRITICAL EMERGENCY - 'TIME IS BRAIN'. Activate the stroke pathway and transfer immediately to a stroke unit: intravenous thrombolysis is indicated within 4.5 hours of onset and mechanical thrombectomy for large vessel occlusion up to 24 hours in selected patients. Check glucose and obtain non-contrast CT before any thrombolysis. Danger signs requiring critical care: reduced or declining level of consciousness
a large MCA territory infarct with midline shift (malignant MCA syndrome - consider decompressive craniectomy)
cerebellar infarct with brainstem compression or hydrocephalus
basilar artery occlusion (fluctuating consciousness, quadriparesis, cranial nerve palsies - very high mortality)
seizures
respiratory compromise or failure to protect the airway
hypoglycaemia (correct immediately). Also urgent: any transient ischaemic attack (up to 10% risk of stroke within a week - assess and treat immediately, do not defer)
stroke in a young patient (investigate for dissection, patent foramen ovale, vasculitis, thrombophilia and drug use)
atrial fibrillation (anticoagulate after the appropriate interval)
carotid stenosis of 50-99% on the symptomatic side (endarterectomy within 2 weeks)
NIL BY MOUTH until a formal SWALLOW SCREEN is done (aspiration pneumonia is a leading cause of death)
avoid lowering blood pressure aggressively in acute ischaemic stroke unless thrombolysis is planned or it exceeds 220/120 mmHg
referralCriteria: Refer to a stroke unit for all patients treated with thrombolysis or thrombectomy
Patients with significant carotid stenosis (>50%) should be evaluated for possible surgical intervention
conditions.firstLine: supportive care - attention to airway, breathing, circulation, and glycemic control.

symptoms.sourceText: Bilateral headache of pressing or tightening (non-pulsating) quality, of mild to moderate intensity, not aggravated by routine physical activity
Often described as a tight band around the head or a weight on top of it
Tightness and aching in the neck, occiput and shoulders

No nausea or vomiting (mild nausea is permitted only in the chronic form), and not more than one of photophobia or phonophobia - the near-absence of these associated features is what distinguishes it from migraine
The headache typically builds slowly through the day and is worse in the evening
The patient can usually continue working
symptoms.masterName: The patient can usually continue working

symptoms.sourceText: Precipitants - mental stress, poor posture, prolonged screen or desk work, eye strain, sleep deprivation, missed meals, dehydration, neck strain and depression
Classified as infrequent episodic (fewer than 1 day a month), frequent episodic (1-14 days a month) or chronic (15 or more days a month for over 3 months)

signs: GENERAL AND NEUROLOGICAL EXAMINATION IS NORMAL - this is essential to the diagnosis. The only positive finding is INCREASED PERICRANIAL TENDERNESS on manual palpation of the frontalis, temporalis, masseter, pterygoid, sternocleidomastoid, splenius and trapezius muscles, elicited by small rotating movements with the second and third fingers

taut bands and trigger points may be palpable in the trapezius and cervical muscles. Check cervical spine range of movement and posture. Examine the FUNDI FOR PAPILLOEDEMA, assess visual acuity and fields, all cranial nerves, limb power, tone, reflexes and plantar responses, coordination and gait

check refraction. The diagnosis is CLINICAL by ICHD-3 criteria - at least 10 episodes with at least two of the four pain characteristics (bilateral, pressing/tightening, mild-moderate, not aggravated by activity), with both no nausea or vomiting and no more than one of photophobia or phonophobia. NEUROIMAGING IS NOT INDICATED when the history is typical and the examination is normal
keep a HEADACHE DIARY and specifically ask about ANALGESIC USE to detect MEDICATION-OVERUSE HEADACHE

redFlags: The same RED FLAGS apply as for any headache and must be excluded: thunderclap onset
headache with fever, neck stiffness or rash
focal neurological deficit, seizure, confusion or personality change
PAPILLOEDEMA or any sign of raised intracranial pressure - headache worse in the morning, on lying flat, or on coughing, sneezing or straining, with vomiting
new or changed headache in a patient over 50 (consider giant cell arteritis - check ESR, ask about scalp tenderness, jaw claudication and visual loss)
headache in an immunocompromised patient or one with cancer or HIV
progressive daily headache that is worsening
headache after head trauma
headache with visual loss, diplopia or pulsatile tinnitus (idiopathic intracranial hypertension - check fundi, especially in a young obese woman)
headache in pregnancy
postural headache
MEDICATION-OVERUSE HEADACHE, which must be recognised and the offending analgesic withdrawn, as it perpetuates chronic daily headache
chronic tension-type headache with significant depression or anxiety needs targeted treatment
failure to respond to simple analgesia and preventive therapy

symptoms.sourceText: An illusion of movement - a spinning, whirling or rotatory sensation of the self or the surroundings (this true rotational quality distinguishes vertigo from light-headedness, presyncope and disequilibrium)
Nystagmus perceived as visual blurring or oscillopsia
A tendency to veer or fall towards one side
symptoms.masterName: Loss of confidence and fear of falling

symptoms.sourceText: Symptoms provoked or worsened by head movement, rolling over in bed, looking up or bending forward
Hearing loss, tinnitus and aural fullness suggesting a peripheral labyrinthine cause (Meniere disease)

In central causes, associated diplopia, dysarthria, dysphagia, facial numbness, limb weakness or ataxia. the time course is the key diagnostic feature - seconds to under a minute with positional change in benign paroxysmal positional vertigo
Minutes to hours with hearing loss, tinnitus and fullness in meniere disease
Days of continuous vertigo after a viral illness in vestibular neuritis (with hearing loss in labyrinthitis)
Minutes with other neurological symptoms in vertebrobasilar TIA
Recurrent attacks with migrainous features in vestibular migraine
Motion sensitivity and sensitivity to visual motion

signs: Examine for NYSTAGMUS - PERIPHERAL nystagmus is horizontal with a torsional component, unidirectional (fast phase away from the affected side), suppressed by visual fixation and fatigable

CENTRAL nystagmus may be purely vertical, purely torsional, direction-changing on gaze, not suppressed by fixation and non-fatigable. The DIX-HALLPIKE MANOEUVRE is diagnostic of posterior canal BPPV, producing, after a latency of 2-20 seconds, a torsional upbeating nystagmus lasting under a minute that fatigues on repetition

the supine roll test identifies horizontal canal BPPV. Perform the HINTS EXAMINATION in acute continuous vertigo, which is more sensitive than early MRI for posterior circulation stroke: HEAD IMPULSE (an ABNORMAL test with a corrective saccade indicates a peripheral lesion, whereas a NORMAL head impulse in a patient with acute vertigo is WORRYING for a central cause), NYSTAGMUS (direction-changing is central), and TEST OF SKEW (any vertical skew deviation on alternate cover testing is central) - 'INFARCT' (Impulse Normal, Fast-phase Alternating, Refixation on Cover Test) indicates a stroke. Also assess: Romberg and Unterberger tests
gait, including tandem gait (inability to walk unaided strongly suggests a central cause)
full cranial nerve examination
cerebellar signs - dysdiadochokinesis, past-pointing, intention tremor
Rinne and Weber tuning fork tests and audiometry
otoscopy for cholesteatoma, effusion or vesicles
the fistula test
lying and standing blood pressure
and cardiac examination for arrhythmia

Brain MRI for central causes of vertigo

redFlags: Refer as an EMERGENCY when a CENTRAL cause is suspected - vertigo with any of the '5 Ds' (dizziness, diplopia, dysarthria, dysphagia, dysmetria) plus ataxia, or with a NORMAL head impulse test, DIRECTION-CHANGING nystagmus, VERTICAL or PURELY TORSIONAL nystagmus, SKEW DEVIATION, INABILITY TO STAND OR WALK UNAIDED, severe headache or neck pain, or any focal neurological sign - this indicates CEREBELLAR OR BRAINSTEM STROKE, and cerebellar infarction can swell and cause fatal brainstem compression and hydrocephalus. Also urgent: sudden vertigo with SUDDEN SENSORINEURAL HEARING LOSS (an otological emergency needing steroids within days)
vertigo after head trauma or neck manipulation (perilymph fistula or vertebral artery dissection)
vertigo with vesicles on the pinna and facial palsy (Ramsay Hunt syndrome)
vertigo with fever, ear discharge and an attic perforation (cholesteatoma with labyrinthine fistula or intracranial spread)
new vertigo in a patient with cardiovascular risk factors
progressive unilateral hearing loss with tinnitus and imbalance (vestibular schwannoma - MRI)
vertigo with papilloedema
intractable vomiting with dehydration
recurrent unexplained falls

symptoms.sourceText: Sudden onset of unilateral facial weakness with drooping of one side of the face
Inability to close the eye on the affected side
Drooping of the angle of the mouth with drooling
Inability to raise the eyebrow, frown or whistle
Food collecting in the affected cheek
symptoms.masterName: Food collecting in the affected cheek

symptoms.sourceText: Watering of the eye or, conversely, dryness and grittiness
Pain behind or below the ear preceding the weakness by 1-2 days
Altered taste on the anterior two-thirds of the tongue (chorda tympani involvement)
Hyperacusis or intolerance of loud sounds (nerve to stapedius)
Numbness or a heavy feeling of the face (usually subjective, with normal objective sensation)
Rapid progression to maximum weakness within 72 hours in Bell's palsy

signs: THE SINGLE MOST IMPORTANT DISTINCTION IS UPPER VERSUS LOWER MOTOR NEURON. In LOWER MOTOR NEURON (peripheral) palsy - Bell's palsy, Ramsay Hunt, otitis media, parotid tumour, trauma - THE WHOLE HALF OF THE FACE INCLUDING THE FOREHEAD IS PARALYSED: the patient cannot wrinkle the forehead or raise the eyebrow on the affected side. In UPPER MOTOR NEURON palsy (stroke or other supranuclear lesion) THE FOREHEAD IS SPARED because of bilateral cortical innervation of the upper face, and emotional (spontaneous) smiling may be preserved while voluntary movement is lost. Test each branch: raise the eyebrows (frontalis), close the eyes tightly against resistance (orbicularis oculi), show the teeth and smile (zygomaticus and buccinator), purse the lips and whistle, blow out the cheeks, and tense the neck (platysma). Look for BELL'S PHENOMENON - upward rolling of the globe on attempted eye closure, with incomplete lid closure and a visible sclera. Grade severity by the HOUSE-BRACKMANN scale I to VI. Examine the EAR AND MASTOID CAREFULLY - otoscopy for otitis media, cholesteatoma or a discharging ear, and inspect the pinna, external canal, palate and anterior tongue for the VESICLES of RAMSAY HUNT SYNDROME (herpes zoster oticus, which also causes vertigo and sensorineural hearing loss). Palpate the PAROTID GLAND for a mass. Test taste on the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, corneal sensation and the corneal reflex, hearing with tuning forks, and ALL OTHER CRANIAL NERVES
examine limb power, reflexes, plantar responses and gait
check blood pressure and blood glucose
examine for a rash or tick bite and enquire about Lyme disease exposure
look for parotid or facial swelling, lymphadenopathy and, in bilateral cases, for sarcoidosis, Lyme disease, HIV, Guillain-Barre syndrome and Melkersson-Rosenthal syndrome

redFlags: FOREHEAD SPARING - an upper motor neuron pattern is a STROKE until proven otherwise: assess urgently on the stroke pathway, particularly with associated limb weakness, dysphasia or a sudden onset. Also urgent referral: facial palsy with OTHER CRANIAL NERVE PALSIES, limb weakness, ataxia, diplopia or altered consciousness (brainstem lesion, tumour or meningeal disease)
BILATERAL facial palsy (Guillain-Barre syndrome, Lyme disease, sarcoidosis, HIV seroconversion, leukaemia, or basal skull fracture - always investigate)
vesicles on the pinna or palate with severe pain, vertigo or hearing loss (RAMSAY HUNT SYNDROME - needs prompt aciclovir plus steroid, and has a worse prognosis than Bell's palsy)
facial palsy with ear discharge, mastoid tenderness or a cholesteatoma (surgical emergency)
a parotid mass (malignancy)
facial palsy after head trauma
SLOWLY PROGRESSIVE weakness over weeks rather than sudden onset, or failure to show ANY recovery by 3-4 months (image to exclude a tumour)
recurrent ipsilateral palsy
facial palsy in a child

INABILITY TO CLOSE THE EYE - the cornea is at immediate risk of exposure keratitis and ulceration, so prescribe lubricants, ointment at night and taping or an eye shield, and refer to ophthalmology if there is pain, redness or reduced vision
facial palsy in pregnancy, diabetes or immunosuppression
conditions.firstLine: Prednisone 60-80 mg daily during the first 5 days and then tapered over the next 5 days, modestly shortens recovery and improves the functional outcome.

source.guideline: Harrison's 21e Ch.434 (Diseases of the Cranial Nerves - Bell's Palsy); Robbins & Cotran 10e Ch.27; WHO ICD-11 8B88.0

symptoms.sourceText: Physical and psychological symptoms arising in temporal relation to an identifiable stressor - tension headache, muscle aches especially of the neck and shoulders, fatigue, palpitations, chest tightness, breathlessness, abdominal discomfort and disturbed sleep
Feeling overwhelmed, tense or unable to cope
Loss of interest and reduced motivation
symptoms.masterName: Loss of interest and reduced motivation

symptoms.sourceText: Exacerbation of pre-existing conditions such as asthma, eczema, psoriasis, irritable bowel syndrome, migraine and hypertension
Increased use of alcohol, tobacco or other substances

In adjustment disorder, these symptoms begin within a month of an identifiable psychosocial stressor (bereavement, job loss, illness diagnosis, financial or relationship difficulty, migration) and cause significant impairment, being preoccupied with the stressor and failing to adapt
In burnout, the triad of emotional exhaustion, cynicism or depersonalisation towards one's work, and reduced professional efficacy

signs: Examination is directed at EXCLUDING ORGANIC DISEASE and is otherwise normal or shows only non-specific findings - tachycardia, mildly raised blood pressure, cool sweaty palms, tremor, tense pericranial and trapezius muscles with palpable trigger points, and sighing respiration. Take a full history of the stressor, its timing, the person's coping resources, social support, and the impact on function. ASSESS MOOD, ANXIETY AND SUICIDE RISK FORMALLY - use PHQ-9 and GAD-7 - because adjustment disorder, depression and anxiety overlap and the distinction determines management

establish whether criteria for a depressive or anxiety disorder are actually met, as stress-related symptoms alone do not warrant antidepressant therapy. SCREEN FOR ALCOHOL AND SUBSTANCE MISUSE with AUDIT-C or CAGE. ASK DIRECTLY ABOUT DOMESTIC VIOLENCE, ABUSE, BULLYING AND HARASSMENT in a private setting, as these commonly underlie 'stress' presentations and are otherwise missed. EXCLUDE organic mimics with targeted investigation - thyroid function, full blood count, glucose, renal and liver function, and ECG where there are cardiac symptoms
investigate any red flag symptom on its own merits rather than attributing it to stress.
Fever, myalgias, and sore throat

tests.sourceText: PHQ-9
GAD-7
AUDIT-C
CAGE
Examination directed at excluding organic disease
Thyroid function tests
Full blood count
Glucose test
Renal function tests
Liver function tests
ECG if there are cardiac symptoms

redFlags: SUICIDAL IDEATION, SELF-HARM OR THOUGHTS OF HARMING OTHERS - assess urgently and do not leave the person alone if the risk is acute. Also urgent: disclosure of DOMESTIC VIOLENCE, ABUSE OR NEGLECT (adult or child safeguarding referral)
symptoms following a major traumatic event with flashbacks, nightmares, dissociation and hypervigilance persisting beyond a month (POST-TRAUMATIC STRESS DISORDER - needs trauma-focused therapy)
psychotic symptoms or severe agitation
a full depressive or anxiety disorder rather than a transient stress reaction (treat accordingly)
escalating alcohol or substance use, or withdrawal symptoms
severe functional impairment with inability to work or care for dependants
complicated or prolonged grief
symptoms persisting beyond 6 months after the stressor has resolved (reconsider the diagnosis)

NEVER ATTRIBUTE NEW OR PROGRESSIVE PHYSICAL SYMPTOMS TO STRESS WITHOUT ADEQUATE ASSESSMENT - weight loss, fever, night sweats, haemoptysis, chest pain, focal neurological signs, a lump, or a change in bowel habit all require investigation in their own right
stress-related presentation in a person with chronic disease and deteriorating control (diabetes, asthma, hypertension)
pregnancy and the postpartum period
Nausea severe enough to cause dehydration
referralCriteria: refer for psychotherapy if symptoms persist or worsen despite supportive care.
refer to psychiatry if there is significant overlap with depressive or anxiety disorders.
conditions.firstLine: supportive care - assess mood, anxiety and suicide risk formally

source.guideline: Harrison's 21e Ch.452; ICD-11 6B40-6B4Z (Disorders Specifically Associated with Stress) and QD85 (Burnout); WHO mhGAP Intervention Guide

symptoms.sourceText: Often asymptomatic in the early stages and detected on screening
As it progresses - fatigue and weakness
symptoms.masterName: As it progresses - fatigue and weakness

symptoms.sourceText: A metallic taste in the mouth and uraemic fetor
Peripheral neuropathy with numbness and tingling
Polyuria then oliguria in advanced disease

Causes to elicit - diabetes mellitus and hypertension account for most cases, followed by glomerulonephritis, polycystic kidney disease, obstructive uropathy, recurrent pyelonephritis, and long-term nsaid or nephrotoxin exposure

signs: PALLOR from normocytic normochromic ANAEMIA of erythropoietin deficiency
HYPERTENSION is present in the great majority and is both cause and consequence
PERIORBITAL AND PEDAL PITTING OEDEMA
raised jugular venous pressure and basal crackles in fluid overload
sallow, yellow-brown skin pigmentation with excoriations from scratching
uraemic fetor
pericardial friction rub in advanced uraemia
ASTERIXIS, myoclonus, confusion and, ultimately, seizures and coma in uraemic encephalopathy
peripheral neuropathy with absent ankle jerks
proximal myopathy and bone tenderness
ballotable enlarged kidneys in POLYCYSTIC KIDNEY DISEASE
a palpable bladder or enlarged prostate in obstruction
abdominal or renal bruit in renovascular disease
features of the underlying disease - diabetic retinopathy on fundoscopy is an important clue to diabetic nephropathy
assess vascular access sites and check for a dialysis fistula thrill and bruit.

tests.sourceText: serum creatinine with eGFR, urea, electrolytes with POTASSIUM
bicarbonate (metabolic acidosis)
calcium, PHOSPHATE, parathyroid hormone and vitamin D (CKD-mineral and bone disorder)
haemoglobin, ferritin and transferrin saturation
albumin, lipids, HbA1c
urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio
urine microscopy for casts (red cell casts indicate glomerulonephritis)

ULTRASOUND showing small, shrunken, echogenic kidneys with loss of corticomedullary differentiation in established CKD (normal or large kidneys suggest diabetes, amyloid, polycystic disease, HIV nephropathy or obstruction)

redFlags: HYPERKALAEMIA with potassium above 6.0-6.5 mmol/L or ECG changes - peaked T waves, a widened QRS, a flattened or absent P wave, or a sine wave pattern - is IMMEDIATELY LIFE-THREATENING and requires calcium gluconate for cardiac protection, insulin-dextrose, salbutamol and urgent dialysis. Also emergency: PULMONARY OEDEMA unresponsive to diuretics
SEVERE METABOLIC ACIDOSIS with a bicarbonate below 15 mmol/L and Kussmaul respiration
URAEMIC PERICARDITIS with chest pain and a rub, which risks tamponade
uraemic ENCEPHALOPATHY with confusion, asterixis, seizures or coma
and refractory fluid overload - each of these is an INDICATION FOR URGENT DIALYSIS
eGFR below 30 (stage G4 - plan for renal replacement therapy, vascular access and transplant assessment)
heavy proteinuria with an ACR above 70 mg/mmol, or nephrotic syndrome with oedema, hypoalbuminaemia and hyperlipidaemia
persistent haematuria with proteinuria or red cell casts (glomerulonephritis - needs biopsy)
uncontrolled hypertension on four agents
suspected renal artery stenosis, particularly a rise in creatinine of more than 30% after starting an ACE inhibitor or ARB
hereditary kidney disease
suspected obstruction on ultrasound (urological emergency if infected)
symptomatic anaemia
severe CKD-MBD with a rising PTH
and AVOID nephrotoxins - NSAIDs, aminoglycosides, and contrast media without precautions - and DOSE-ADJUST ALL DRUGS for renal function
referralCriteria: if repeat testing shows declining GFR, albuminuria, or uncontrolled hypertension, referral to a nephrologist is appropriate.
conditions.firstLine: supportive care - dietary salt restriction and the use of loop diuretics, occasionally in combination with metolazone.

rx.titration: dose-adjust based on response and renal function
rx.renalAdjust: dose adjustment needed based on renal function
rx.paediatricDose: consider lower doses depending on renal function

documentation and guidelines on chronic kidney disease

source.guideline: Harrison's 21e Ch.311 (Chronic Kidney Disease); KDIGO Guidelines; Robbins & Cotran 10e Ch.20 (The Kidney); WHO ICD-11 GB61

symptoms.sourceText: An abrupt decline in kidney function over hours to days - oliguria (urine output less than 0.5 mL/kg/h or under 400 mL a day) or anuria, though it may be non-oliguric
Swelling of the legs and face
symptoms.masterName: Swelling of the legs and face

symptoms.sourceText: Confusion, drowsiness and, in severe uraemia, seizures
Symptoms of the precipitating cause - diarrhoea, vomiting, bleeding, burns or sepsis (prerenal)
A recent nephrotoxic drug such as an nsaid, ACE inhibitor, ARB, aminoglycoside, contrast medium, amphotericin or a herbal remedy
Muscle pain with dark cola-coloured urine after crush injury, prolonged immobility, seizures or statin use (rhabdomyolysis)
Rash, fever and eosinophilia after a new drug (acute interstitial nephritis)
Bloody diarrhoea followed by pallor and bruising in a child (haemolytic uraemic syndrome)
Poor stream, hesitancy and a history of prostatic symptoms, or complete anuria (postrenal obstruction)
Fever with rigors and loin pain (pyelonephritis)

signs: ASSESS VOLUME STATUS FIRST, as this determines management: in HYPOVOLAEMIA there is tachycardia, postural or frank HYPOTENSION, a low jugular venous pressure, dry mucous membranes, reduced skin turgor, delayed capillary refill, cool peripheries and concentrated urine

in HYPERVOLAEMIA there is a raised JVP, peripheral and sacral oedema, basal crackles, a third heart sound and hypertension. Look for a PALPABLE BLADDER and perform a DIGITAL RECTAL EXAMINATION for prostatic enlargement - and CATHETERISE EARLY, since relieving obstruction is immediately curative. Examine for signs of sepsis, an abdominal aortic aneurysm, abdominal compartment syndrome, a renal bruit, and rash or livedo reticularis (vasculitis, cholesterol emboli)

check for asterixis, confusion and a pericardial RUB (uraemia). STAGE BY KDIGO CRITERIA: Stage 1 - creatinine rise of 26.5 micromol/L (0.3 mg/dL) within 48 hours or a 1.5-1.9 fold rise from baseline within 7 days, or urine output under 0.5 mL/kg/h for 6-12 hours
Stage 2 - 2.0-2.9 fold rise or output under 0.5 mL/kg/h for over 12 hours

Stage 3 - 3 fold rise, creatinine above 353.6 micromol/L, initiation of renal replacement therapy, or output under 0.3 mL/kg/h for 24 hours or anuria for 12 hours. Investigate: urea, creatinine, ELECTROLYTES WITH URGENT POTASSIUM, bicarbonate, calcium, phosphate, full blood count, CRP, blood cultures, creatine kinase, LDH, blood film for fragmented cells, coagulation, blood gas, urinalysis and microscopy (muddy-brown granular casts in acute tubular necrosis, red cell casts in glomerulonephritis, white cell casts and eosinophiluria in interstitial nephritis, and a bland sediment in prerenal disease), urine sodium and fractional excretion of sodium (below 1% in prerenal), ANCA, anti-GBM, ANA, complement and myeloma screen where indicated, and URGENT ULTRASOUND TO EXCLUDE OBSTRUCTION IN EVERY CASE
ECG for hyperkalaemia
Look for fever, chills, changes in mental status, and signs suggesting acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS)

tests.sourceText: check for asterixis, confusion and a pericardial RUB (uraemia). STAGE BY KDIGO CRITERIA

urea, creatinine, ELECTROLYTES WITH URGENT POTASSIUM, bicarbonate, calcium, phosphate, full blood count, CRP, blood cultures, creatine kinase, LDH, blood film for fragmented cells, coagulation, blood gas, urinalysis and microscopy (muddy-brown granular casts in acute tubular necrosis, red cell casts in glomerulonephritis, white cell casts and eosinophiluria in interstitial nephritis, and a bland sediment in prerenal disease), urine sodium and fractional excretion of sodium (below 1% in prerenal), ANCA, anti-GBM, ANA, complement and myeloma screen where indicated, and URGENT ULTRASOUND TO EXCLUDE OBSTRUCTION IN EVERY CASE
ECG for hyperkalaemia

redFlags: ACUTE KIDNEY INJURY IS A MEDICAL EMERGENCY. IMMEDIATE THREATS: HYPERKALAEMIA with potassium above 6.5 mmol/L or ECG changes (tall tented T waves, small or absent P waves, broad QRS, sine wave) - give intravenous CALCIUM GLUCONATE for myocardial protection, then insulin-dextrose and nebulised salbutamol, and arrange urgent dialysis
PULMONARY OEDEMA unresponsive to diuretics
severe METABOLIC ACIDOSIS with pH below 7.1
uraemic ENCEPHALOPATHY, seizures or PERICARDITIS

and refractory fluid overload - these constitute the classical indications for URGENT RENAL REPLACEMENT THERAPY (remembered as A-E-I-O-U: Acidosis, Electrolytes, Intoxication, Overload, Uraemia). Also act immediately on: OBSTRUCTION on ultrasound (catheterise, or arrange nephrostomy or stenting - an obstructed infected system is a urological emergency)
SEPSIS (cultures and antibiotics within one hour)
hypovolaemic shock (fluid resuscitation)
rhabdomyolysis with a very high creatine kinase (aggressive fluids)
haemoptysis with haematuria and acute kidney injury (pulmonary-renal syndrome from ANCA vasculitis or Goodpasture disease - needs urgent immunosuppression and possibly plasma exchange)
rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (biopsy urgently)
haemolytic uraemic syndrome or thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (anaemia, thrombocytopenia, fragmented cells)
poisoning. ALWAYS STOP NEPHROTOXINS AND REVIEW EVERY DRUG FOR RENAL DOSING - suspend NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, ARBs, diuretics and metformin
withhold contrast where possible
monitor urine output hourly and weigh daily
conditions.firstLine: supportive care - maintain fluid and electrolyte balance while monitoring for complications.

source.guideline: Harrison's 22e Ch.321 (Acute Kidney Injury); KDIGO AKI Guidelines; Robbins & Cotran 10e Ch.20 (Acute Tubular Injury); WHO ICD-11 GB60

symptoms.sourceText: Renal colic - sudden-onset, severe, colicky pain in the loin radiating around the flank to the groin, testis or labia ('loin to groin'), coming in waves of excruciating intensity
The patient is characteristically restless and unable to lie still, writhing and rolling about (in contrast to peritonitis, where the patient lies motionless)
Haematuria, visible in about a third and microscopic in most
Urinary frequency, urgency and strangury as the stone approaches the vesicoureteric junction
Abdominal distension and reduced bowel sounds from reflex ileus
Fever and rigors if infection supervenes
symptoms.masterName: Fever and rigors if infection supervenes

symptoms.sourceText: Staghorn calculi may be asymptomatic or present with recurrent infection

Risk factors - low fluid intake, hot climate and dehydration, high animal protein, salt and oxalate intake, obesity, hypercalcaemia and hyperparathyroidism, hyperuricaemia and gout, recurrent urinary infection with urea-splitting organisms (struvite stones), inflammatory bowel disease and malabsorption, renal tubular acidosis, cystinuria, and drugs such as indinavir and topiramate
Fever, rigors, and flank pain may occur in pyelonephritis

signs: The patient is in obvious distress, pale, sweating and constantly moving
tachycardia and mildly raised blood pressure from pain
low-grade fever may occur from the stone alone, but a HIGH fever with rigors indicates infection. There is marked RENAL ANGLE TENDERNESS and tenderness along the line of the ureter
the abdomen is soft with NO GUARDING OR REBOUND (the absence of peritonism is an important discriminator)

bowel sounds may be reduced. Examine the testes to exclude TORSION, which is the critical differential in a young man with groin pain, and always consider a LEAKING ABDOMINAL AORTIC ANEURYSM in anyone over 50 with first-episode 'renal colic' - palpate for an expansile mass and check femoral pulses. URINALYSIS shows haematuria in about 85% (its ABSENCE does not exclude a stone, particularly with complete obstruction), and nitrites and leucocytes suggest infection

check urine pH (persistently below 5.5 favours uric acid stones, above 7.2 favours struvite). NON-CONTRAST CT OF THE KIDNEYS, URETERS AND BLADDER IS THE INVESTIGATION OF CHOICE with near-100% sensitivity, identifying the stone's size, site and density and any hydronephrosis
ultrasound is preferred in PREGNANCY and in children

plain KUB radiography shows radio-opaque calcium stones but MISSES URIC ACID STONES, which are radiolucent. Check full blood count, CRP, urea, creatinine and electrolytes, calcium, uric acid and, in recurrent stone formers, parathyroid hormone and a 24-hour urine collection
send any passed stone for analysis. Stones under 5 mm pass spontaneously in about 80% of cases, those over 10 mm rarely do

redFlags: AN OBSTRUCTED, INFECTED KIDNEY IS A UROLOGICAL EMERGENCY - fever with rigors, loin pain and hydronephrosis, with or without hypotension and confusion, indicates PYONEPHROSIS AND URINARY SEPSIS, which can be rapidly fatal

antibiotics alone are inadequate and IMMEDIATE DECOMPRESSION by percutaneous nephrostomy or retrograde stenting is required. Also emergency or urgent: ANURIA or acute kidney injury (bilateral obstruction, or obstruction of a single functioning or transplanted kidney)
uncontrolled pain despite adequate analgesia
intractable vomiting with dehydration
a stone larger than 10 mm, or failure to pass a smaller stone within 4-6 weeks
RENAL COLIC IN PREGNANCY
renal colic in a child
a solitary kidney
bilateral obstructing stones
suspected LEAKING ABDOMINAL AORTIC ANEURYSM masquerading as renal colic in an older patient (this misdiagnosis is a classic and lethal error - have a low threshold for imaging)
TESTICULAR TORSION in a young man with groin pain and a tender high-riding testis with an absent cremasteric reflex (surgical emergency within 6 hours)
ectopic pregnancy in a woman of reproductive age
recurrent stone formation or a staghorn calculus (needs metabolic evaluation and definitive urological management)
and always advise high fluid intake of 2.5-3 litres a day to prevent recurrence, which is otherwise around 50% within 5-10 years
conditions.firstLine: supportive care - advise high fluid intake of 2.5-3 litres a day to prevent recurrence.

source.guideline: Harrison's 21e Ch.315 (Nephrolithiasis); Robbins & Cotran 10e Ch.20 (Urolithiasis); WHO ICD-11 GB70

symptoms.sourceText: Lower urinary tract symptoms in men over 50, comprising voiding (obstructive) symptoms - hesitancy, a weak and poorly sustained stream, straining to void, intermittency, terminal dribbling and a sensation of incomplete emptying - and storage (irritative) symptoms - urinary frequency, urgency, nocturia and urge incontinence
Reduced quality of life with sleep disruption from nocturia and consequent daytime fatigue
Anxiety about access to toilets and social restriction
Acute urinary retention with severe suprapubic pain and inability to pass urine
Chronic retention with painless abdominal distension and overflow incontinence, especially at night
Symptoms worsened by alcohol, cold weather, diuretics, anticholinergics, opioids, antihistamines, decongestants and tricyclic antidepressants
Note that symptom severity correlates poorly with prostate size

signs: ABDOMINAL EXAMINATION for a palpable, dull, percussible suprapubic mass arising out of the pelvis (a distended bladder in chronic retention - it cannot be got below). DIGITAL RECTAL EXAMINATION IS ESSENTIAL and in benign hyperplasia reveals a SMOOTH, SYMMETRICALLY ENLARGED, FIRM-BUT-ELASTIC (rubbery) prostate with a PRESERVED MEDIAN SULCUS and intact mobile overlying rectal mucosa - in contrast to CARCINOMA, which is HARD, NODULAR, IRREGULAR AND ASYMMETRICAL with LOSS OF THE MEDIAN SULCUS, and possibly fixed with extension beyond the capsule. Assess anal tone and perineal sensation to exclude a neurological cause. Examine the external genitalia for meatal stenosis and phimosis. Quantify symptoms with the INTERNATIONAL PROSTATE SYMPTOM SCORE (IPSS) - mild 0-7, moderate 8-19, severe 20-35 - together with the quality-of-life question. Ask the patient to complete a FREQUENCY-VOLUME CHART for 3 days. INVESTIGATIONS: urinalysis and culture to exclude infection and haematuria
serum creatinine and electrolytes to assess for obstructive uropathy

PROSTATE-SPECIFIC ANTIGEN after appropriate counselling about its implications, noting that PSA rises with BPH, prostatitis, infection, catheterisation, recent ejaculation and digital examination as well as with cancer, and is LOWERED by about half by 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors
URINARY FLOW RATE with a maximum flow (Qmax) below 10 mL/s suggesting obstruction
POST-VOID RESIDUAL VOLUME by ultrasound (a residual above 100-200 mL is significant)
transabdominal or transrectal ultrasound for prostate volume and to assess the upper tracts for HYDRONEPHROSIS
urodynamics in equivocal cases

redFlags: ACUTE URINARY RETENTION - painful inability to void with a palpable tender bladder, requiring immediate catheterisation. HIGH-PRESSURE CHRONIC RETENTION with a grossly distended painless bladder, bilateral HYDRONEPHROSIS and RENAL IMPAIRMENT - catheterise and monitor closely for POST-OBSTRUCTIVE DIURESIS, which can cause profound fluid and electrolyte loss and hypotension. Also refer urgently: any HARD, NODULAR OR ASYMMETRIC PROSTATE, or a raised or rapidly rising PSA (suspected PROSTATE CANCER - urgent two-week-wait referral for MRI and biopsy)
VISIBLE HAEMATURIA at any age (exclude bladder and renal malignancy)
back or bone pain with a raised PSA (metastatic disease - and beware SPINAL CORD COMPRESSION)
renal impairment attributable to obstruction
severe symptoms refractory to medical therapy (refer for TURP or other surgery)
a neurological cause suggested by saddle anaesthesia, lower limb weakness, altered anal tone or bowel dysfunction (CAUDA EQUINA SYNDROME - emergency)
conditions.firstLine: supportive care - manage fluid intake and use alpha-blockers for symptomatic relief.

source.guideline: Harrison's 21e Ch.86 (Benign and Malignant Diseases of the Prostate); Robbins & Cotran 10e Ch.21 (The Prostate - Nodular Hyperplasia); WHO ICD-11 GA90

symptoms.sourceText: Acute bacterial prostatitis - abrupt onset of high fever with rigors, perineal and suprapubic pain, dysuria, urinary frequency and urgency, and difficulty voiding or acute retention, with marked systemic illness. chronic PROSTATITIS/CHRONIC pelvic pain syndrome - persistent pelvic, perineal, suprapubic, penile, testicular or lower back pain for at least 3 of the preceding 6 months, with urinary symptoms
Pain on ejaculation and painful or bloody ejaculate (haematospermia)
Pain radiating to the rectum, groin, penile tip or inner thighs
Pain aggravated by sitting for long periods or by cycling
A sensation of incomplete bladder emptying
Myalgia and arthralgia in the acute form
symptoms.masterName: Myalgia and arthralgia in the acute form

symptoms.sourceText: Anxiety, depression and significant impairment of quality of life are prominent in the chronic form
Risk factors - recent urethral instrumentation or catheterisation, transrectal prostate biopsy, unprotected anal intercourse, urethral stricture, bladder outflow obstruction and diabetes
Classified by the nih system into I acute bacterial, ii chronic bacterial, IIIa inflammatory and IIIb non-inflammatory chronic pelvic pain syndrome, and IV asymptomatic inflammatory prostatitis
Acute bacterial prostatitis is a severe illness that can be accompanied by fever and rigors

signs: In ACUTE BACTERIAL PROSTATITIS the patient is febrile, tachycardic and unwell, with suprapubic tenderness and sometimes a palpable distended bladder. DIGITAL RECTAL EXAMINATION reveals an EXQUISITELY TENDER, HOT, SWOLLEN AND BOGGY PROSTATE - and VIGOROUS PROSTATIC MASSAGE MUST BE AVOIDED IN THE ACUTE PHASE because it is intensely painful and may precipitate bacteraemia. In CHRONIC PROSTATITIS the prostate may feel normal, mildly tender, or boggy, and there is often tenderness of the pelvic floor musculature, the levator ani and the coccyx, with palpable myofascial trigger points. Examine the external genitalia and epididymes to exclude epididymo-orchitis, and the abdomen for a distended bladder. INVESTIGATIONS: urinalysis, MIDSTREAM URINE MICROSCOPY AND CULTURE, and BLOOD CULTURES in the acute form
full blood count showing leucocytosis, and raised CRP
a markedly RAISED PSA is common in acute prostatitis and should NOT be measured during the acute episode, nor interpreted as cancer - repeat it at least 4-6 weeks after resolution
NAAT for Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae in younger, sexually active men
the MEARES-STAMEY FOUR-GLASS TEST or the simpler two-glass pre- and post-massage test localises infection to the prostate in the chronic bacterial form
measure post-void residual volume
transrectal ultrasound or CT if abscess is suspected
use the NIH-CHRONIC PROSTATITIS SYMPTOM INDEX to quantify symptoms and monitor response

transrectal ultrasound or CT if abscess is suspected

redFlags: SEPSIS - high fever with rigors, tachycardia, hypotension and confusion (acute bacterial prostatitis is a recognised cause of Gram-negative SEPSIS and bacteraemia - take cultures and give antibiotics urgently and admit). ACUTE URINARY RETENTION complicating acute prostatitis - AVOID URETHRAL CATHETERISATION where possible, as it is very painful and may worsen the infection

SUPRAPUBIC CATHETERISATION is preferred. PROSTATIC ABSCESS - suspect when there is persistent high fever, worsening pain and a fluctuant area on rectal examination despite 48-72 hours of appropriate antibiotics, particularly in diabetic or immunocompromised men (needs imaging and drainage). Also refer: failure to respond to appropriate antibiotics
recurrent episodes (chronic bacterial prostatitis needs a prolonged 4-6 week course of a fluoroquinolone or trimethoprim, since most antibiotics penetrate the prostate poorly)
prostatitis after transrectal biopsy (often resistant organisms)
a persistently raised PSA more than 6 weeks after resolution, or a hard nodular prostate (exclude PROSTATE CANCER)
haematuria (exclude urological malignancy)
prostatitis in a diabetic or immunocompromised patient
suspected sexually transmitted infection (screen fully and treat partners)
severe chronic pelvic pain with depression or suicidal ideation (needs multidisciplinary pain management)
and always exclude other causes of the acute scrotum and pelvic pain

symptoms.sourceText: Polyuria with the passage of large volumes of dilute, colourless urine, typically more than 3 litres a day and often 5-20 litres
Intense polydipsia with a craving for cold water
Nocturia and nocturnal thirst that disturb sleep
Fatigue and daytime sleepiness from disrupted sleep
Dehydration with dry mouth and skin if access to water is restricted
In infants and young children - unexplained fever, vomiting, constipation, failure to thrive, irritability and developmental delay, since they cannot express thirst
Headache and visual field disturbance if a hypothalamic or pituitary tumour is responsible
Features of associated anterior pituitary failure - amenorrhoea, loss of libido, fatigue, cold intolerance and postural dizziness

Causes: central (cranial) diabetes insipidus from deficient vasopressin secretion due to pituitary or hypothalamic surgery, head injury, craniopharyngioma, germinoma, metastases, Langerhans cell histiocytosis, sarcoidosis, tuberculosis, lymphocytic hypophysitis, Sheehan syndrome or familial disease

Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus from renal resistance to vasopressin due to lithium (the commonest acquired cause), hypercalcaemia, hypokalaemia, chronic kidney disease, obstructive uropathy, sickle cell disease, demeclocycline or inherited AVPR2/aquaporin-2 mutations
And primary polydipsia from excessive water intake, often psychogenic

signs: The patient may appear well or show signs of DEHYDRATION - dry mucous membranes, reduced skin turgor, sunken eyes, tachycardia, postural hypotension and a low jugular venous pressure - particularly if thirst is impaired or water is unavailable. Assess for visual field defects by confrontation (BITEMPORAL HEMIANOPIA from a suprasellar lesion compressing the optic chiasm), cranial nerve palsies, and features of hypopituitarism
examine growth and development in children. INVESTIGATIONS: confirm true polyuria with a 24-HOUR URINE VOLUME above 3 litres (or 40-50 mL/kg)

simultaneous serum and urine osmolality shows a LOW URINE OSMOLALITY (typically below 300 mOsm/kg and often below 200) with a HIGH-NORMAL OR RAISED SERUM OSMOLALITY (above 295 mOsm/kg) and a serum SODIUM at the upper limit or frankly raised - the combination of hypernatraemia with dilute urine is virtually diagnostic

in primary polydipsia the serum sodium and osmolality are LOW. THE WATER DEPRIVATION TEST WITH DESMOPRESSIN remains the classical confirmatory test and MUST BE PERFORMED UNDER CLOSE SUPERVISION WITH HOURLY WEIGHT, OSMOLALITY AND SODIUM MONITORING, and stopped if weight falls by more than 3-5%: in normal subjects and primary polydipsia the urine concentrates above 750 mOsm/kg
in CENTRAL diabetes insipidus the urine remains dilute after deprivation but CONCENTRATES BY MORE THAN 50% AFTER DESMOPRESSIN

in NEPHROGENIC disease it fails to concentrate after both. Measurement of COPEPTIN, particularly after arginine or hypertonic saline stimulation, has now largely superseded the water deprivation test where available. Also check calcium, potassium, glucose (to exclude diabetes mellitus, the far commoner cause of polyuria), renal function, and lithium levels

MRI OF THE PITUITARY AND HYPOTHALAMUS is mandatory in central disease and characteristically shows LOSS OF THE NORMAL POSTERIOR PITUITARY BRIGHT SPOT on T1-weighted imaging, and may reveal a tumour, thickened stalk or infiltrative lesion
assess full anterior pituitary function

simultaneous serum and urine osmolality tests

redFlags: SEVERE HYPERNATRAEMIA AND HYPOVOLAEMIC SHOCK if fluid intake is interrupted - this is the principal danger, and it arises whenever thirst or access to water is impaired: in the UNCONSCIOUS PATIENT, the very young, the elderly, those with hypothalamic damage causing ADIPSIA, patients who are nil by mouth, and perioperatively. Such patients can lose litres of urine per hour and become critically hypernatraemic within hours - they require hourly monitoring of urine output, sodium and osmolality with meticulous fluid replacement. Note also that CORRECTING HYPERNATRAEMIA TOO RAPIDLY RISKS CEREBRAL OEDEMA, so lower the sodium by no more than 10-12 mmol/L in 24 hours. Other red flags: new-onset diabetes insipidus with HEADACHE AND VISUAL FIELD LOSS (suprasellar mass - urgent MRI and neurosurgical referral)
diabetes insipidus after head injury or pituitary surgery, which may follow a TRIPHASIC pattern of DI, then SIADH, then permanent DI (monitor sodium closely)

associated anterior pituitary hormone deficiency, particularly ADRENAL INSUFFICIENCY, which must be treated first - CORTISOL DEFICIENCY CAN MASK DIABETES INSIPIDUS, so polyuria may appear or worsen only after starting hydrocortisone
diabetes insipidus in pregnancy (transient gestational DI from placental vasopressinase, and an association with pre-eclampsia and acute fatty liver)
hypercalcaemia or lithium toxicity as a cause (review the drug with the prescribing psychiatrist - lithium-induced nephrogenic DI may be irreversible)
diabetes insipidus in a child with growth failure (exclude craniopharyngioma and histiocytosis)
and never confuse it with DIABETES MELLITUS - always check the blood glucose first in any patient with polyuria and polydipsia
referralCriteria: patients with severe hypernatraemia or hypovolemic shock
diabetes insipidus after head injury or pituitary surgery
new-onset diabetes insipidus with headache and visual field loss

symptoms.sourceText: A prodromal phase of fever, marked anorexia, nausea, vomiting, malaise and fatigue lasting several days to a week, followed by the icteric phase with jaundice (yellow sclerae and skin), dark urine and pale (clay-coloured) stools
Right upper quadrant discomfort or a dragging ache
A distinctive aversion to smoking and to fatty food
symptoms.masterName: Aversion to fatty food and cigarettes

symptoms.sourceText: Low-grade fever that typically settles as jaundice appears
Marked fatigue that may persist for weeks
Most infections in young children are anicteric and asymptomatic, whereas the likelihood of symptomatic and severe disease rises with age
Transmitted by the FAECO-ORAL route through contaminated water, ice, shellfish and food handled by an infected person, and by person-to-person spread in households and institutions
Infectivity is highest in the 2 weeks before jaundice appears
The illness is SELF-LIMITING and does not become chronic, although a relapsing or prolonged cholestatic course occurs in a minority

signs: JAUNDICE - examine the sclerae in natural light, as scleral icterus appears at a bilirubin of about 2.5-3 mg/dL and precedes visible skin jaundice
SMOOTH, TENDER HEPATOMEGALY in the majority
mild SPLENOMEGALY in about 10-20%
posterior cervical lymphadenopathy
scratch marks in cholestatic disease
low-grade fever
bradycardia may accompany deep jaundice

the urine is dark (conjugated bilirubinuria) and the stools pale. IMPORTANTLY, THERE ARE NO STIGMATA OF CHRONIC LIVER DISEASE - no spider naevi, palmar erythema, clubbing, gynaecomastia, testicular atrophy, ascites or caput medusae - and their presence should prompt reconsideration of the diagnosis. LABORATORY: MARKEDLY RAISED TRANSAMINASES, typically 10 to 100 times the upper limit of normal with ALT USUALLY EXCEEDING AST (values of 1000-3000 IU/L are common and peak just before or as jaundice appears)
raised conjugated and unconjugated BILIRUBIN
alkaline phosphatase is normal or only modestly raised except in the cholestatic variant
PROTHROMBIN TIME/INR IS THE SINGLE MOST IMPORTANT PROGNOSTIC TEST and should be checked in every patient
albumin is normal in acute disease

there may be a mild leucopenia with relative lymphocytosis. DIAGNOSIS IS CONFIRMED BY ANTI-HAV IgM, which is positive from the onset of symptoms and persists for 3-6 months, while anti-HAV IgG indicates past infection or vaccination and confers lifelong immunity. Ultrasound is normal or shows a mildly enlarged liver and a thickened gallbladder wall, and is used to exclude biliary obstruction

redFlags: ACUTE LIVER FAILURE (fulminant hepatitis) occurs in under 1% overall but is much commoner in those over 50 and in patients with PRE-EXISTING CHRONIC LIVER DISEASE, especially chronic hepatitis B or C - suspect it with any of: ALTERED MENTAL STATE, from subtle confusion, inverted sleep pattern or personality change through to drowsiness and coma (HEPATIC ENCEPHALOPATHY)
ASTERIXIS (flapping tremor)
a PROLONGED PROTHROMBIN TIME OR INR ABOVE 1.5 NOT CORRECTED BY VITAMIN K
hypoglycaemia
a rapidly SHRINKING LIVER with falling transaminases and rising bilirubin (an ominous combination)
fetor hepaticus
bleeding
and this constitutes a medical emergency requiring urgent referral to a liver transplant centre. Also refer or admit: persistent vomiting with inability to maintain hydration
jaundice deepening beyond 2-3 weeks or lasting more than 3 months (cholestatic variant)
ascites or oedema
a bilirubin above 15-20 mg/dL
PREGNANCY (higher risk of complications)
infants and the elderly
immunocompromised patients

and any patient with underlying chronic liver disease. PUBLIC HEALTH: hepatitis A is a NOTIFIABLE disease - report it, and arrange POST-EXPOSURE PROPHYLAXIS with vaccine (or immunoglobulin in infants under 1 year, the immunocompromised and those with chronic liver disease) for household and close contacts within 14 days
emphasise hand hygiene, safe water and sanitation, exclusion of the patient from food handling, childcare and healthcare work until 7 days after the onset of jaundice
AVOID ALCOHOL and hepatotoxic drugs, and use PARACETAMOL ONLY IN REDUCED DOSE
vaccination is highly effective and gives long-lasting protection

symptoms.sourceText: Acute infection: a prodrome of malaise, anorexia, nausea, vomiting and right upper quadrant discomfort followed by jaundice, dark urine and pale stools - though up to 70% of acute infections are anicteric or subclinical. chronic infection is usually asymptomatic for decades and is detected on screening or when cirrhosis or hepatocellular carcinoma supervenes

In acute disease - a SERUM-SICKNESS-LIKE prodrome in 10-20% with fever, urticarial rash, symmetrical polyarthritis and, rarely, angioedema, caused by circulating immune complexes and characteristically preceding the jaundice (a feature that helps distinguish it from hepatitis A)
Aversion to fatty food and cigarettes
symptoms.masterName: Aversion to fatty food and cigarettes

symptoms.sourceText: Pruritus. In chronic disease - fatigue is the commonest and often the only symptom, with intermittent right upper quadrant ache, anorexia and malaise
Extrahepatic manifestations include polyarteritis nodosa, membranous and membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis, cryoglobulinaemia, and papular acrodermatitis (Gianotti-Crosti syndrome) in children

Features of decompensation appear late with jaundice, ascites, leg swelling, haematemesis and confusion. transmission is parenteral, sexual and perinatal - unsafe injections and needle-stick injury, transfusion of unscreened blood, injecting drug use, tattooing and unsterile procedures, unprotected intercourse, and MOTHER-TO-CHILD transmission at birth, which is the dominant route in high-prevalence regions and carries a 90% risk of chronicity in the neonate compared with under 5% in immunocompetent adults

signs: ACUTE: jaundice, tender smooth hepatomegaly, occasional splenomegaly and lymphadenopathy, urticarial rash and arthritis in the prodrome

transaminases in the thousands with ALT above AST, raised bilirubin, and an INR that must be monitored. CHRONIC HEPATITIS AND CIRRHOSIS: examine specifically for the STIGMATA OF CHRONIC LIVER DISEASE - spider naevi in the distribution of the superior vena cava, palmar erythema, leuconychia, clubbing, Dupuytren's contracture, gynaecomastia, loss of body hair, testicular atrophy, parotid enlargement, jaundice, scratch marks, easy bruising, a firm irregular liver edge or a small shrunken liver, SPLENOMEGALY and other signs of PORTAL HYPERTENSION including ascites with shifting dullness and a fluid thrill, caput medusae and dilated abdominal veins with flow away from the umbilicus

in DECOMPENSATION, look for ASTERIXIS, fetor hepaticus, confusion and altered sleep pattern (encephalopathy), peripheral oedema and muscle wasting. SEROLOGY IS THE KEY TO INTERPRETATION: HBsAg positive indicates current infection, and PERSISTENCE BEYOND 6 MONTHS DEFINES CHRONIC INFECTION
anti-HBc IgM indicates acute or recent infection
anti-HBc IgG indicates past exposure
HBeAg indicates high replication and high infectivity
anti-HBe suggests seroconversion to a lower replicative state, although HBeAg-negative chronic hepatitis with precore mutants remains active

ANTI-HBs ALONE INDICATES IMMUNITY, from vaccination if anti-HBc is negative and from resolved natural infection if anti-HBc IgG is positive. HBV DNA quantifies viral load and guides treatment. Also assess: ALT and AST, bilirubin, albumin, INR, platelet count (thrombocytopenia is an early marker of portal hypertension), alpha-fetoprotein, ultrasound and elastography (FibroScan) or a fibrosis score for staging
and TEST FOR HEPATITIS D, HEPATITIS C AND HIV COINFECTION in every case

redFlags: ACUTE LIVER FAILURE - encephalopathy, asterixis, INR above 1.5, hypoglycaemia and a shrinking liver (fulminant hepatitis B carries high mortality and needs urgent transplant-centre referral). HBV REACTIVATION IS A CRITICAL AND PREVENTABLE DANGER - any HBsAg-positive or even anti-HBc-positive patient about to receive RITUXIMAB, CHEMOTHERAPY, HIGH-DOSE CORTICOSTEROIDS, TNF INHIBITORS OR OTHER IMMUNOSUPPRESSION MUST BE SCREENED AND GIVEN PROPHYLACTIC ANTIVIRAL COVER, as reactivation can be fulminant and fatal

likewise, NEVER STOP ANTIVIRAL THERAPY ABRUPTLY, which can precipitate a severe flare. Other red flags: DECOMPENSATED CIRRHOSIS with ascites, variceal bleeding (haematemesis and melaena - a medical emergency), spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (fever and abdominal pain with ascites), hepatorenal syndrome or encephalopathy

HEPATOCELLULAR CARCINOMA - weight loss, right upper quadrant pain, a hard nodular liver, a bruit, sudden ascites or a rising alpha-fetoprotein (ALL CHRONIC HBV PATIENTS AT RISK REQUIRE 6-MONTHLY SURVEILLANCE WITH ULTRASOUND AND AFP, and HBV causes hepatocellular carcinoma even WITHOUT cirrhosis)
a sudden ALT flare
coinfection with HEPATITIS D, which markedly worsens prognosis

PREGNANCY - screen every pregnant woman, give ANTIVIRAL THERAPY IN THE THIRD TRIMESTER for high viral load, and ensure the neonate receives HEPATITIS B IMMUNOGLOBULIN AND THE FIRST VACCINE DOSE WITHIN 12 HOURS OF BIRTH, which prevents the great majority of perinatal transmission
needle-stick exposure (give immunoglobulin and vaccine promptly)
and vaccinate all household and sexual contacts
referralCriteria: Refer to a specialist if there is a persistent elevation of transaminases or if liver disease is suspected (e.g., ascites, encephalopathy).

symptoms.sourceText: Acute infection is asymptomatic or mild in 70-80% of cases

When symptomatic there is fatigue, anorexia, nausea, right upper quadrant discomfort and mild jaundice. chronic infection, which follows in 55-85% of those infected, is typically silent for decades and is discovered on screening, on finding abnormal liver enzymes, or when cirrhosis or hepatocellular carcinoma declares itself
Fatigue is the commonest symptom of chronic infection and may be disabling

Extrahepatic manifestations are particularly important in hepatitis C and include mixed cryoglobulinaemia with palpable purpura on the legs, arthralgia, weakness, peripheral neuropathy and membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis
Porphyria cutanea tarda with skin fragility and blistering on sun-exposed areas

Transmission is predominantly BLOOD-BORNE - injecting drug use with shared equipment is the dominant route worldwide, along with unsafe therapeutic injections and unsterile medical or dental procedures, transfusion of unscreened blood before the 1990s, haemodialysis, needle-stick injury, tattooing and body piercing with unsterile equipment
Sexual transmission is inefficient except among HIV-positive men who have sex with men, and vertical transmission occurs in about 5% and is higher with HIV coinfection

signs: EXAMINATION IS OFTEN COMPLETELY NORMAL in chronic hepatitis C, which is precisely why screening of at-risk groups matters. When present, findings are those of chronic liver disease and portal hypertension - spider naevi, palmar erythema, leuconychia, clubbing, Dupuytren's contracture, gynaecomastia, testicular atrophy, jaundice, a firm irregular or shrunken liver, SPLENOMEGALY, ascites with shifting dullness, caput medusae, peripheral oedema, asterixis and confusion in decompensation. Look for extrahepatic signs - PALPABLE PURPURA over the lower limbs and livedo, with peripheral neuropathy (cryoglobulinaemic vasculitis)
blistering, milia, scarring and hypertrichosis on the dorsa of the hands (porphyria cutanea tarda)

violaceous flat-topped polygonal papules with Wickham striae, and oral lacy white lesions (lichen planus). LABORATORY: ALT is often only MILDLY RAISED AND FLUCTUATES, and MAY BE PERSISTENTLY NORMAL IN UP TO A THIRD OF PATIENTS DESPITE SIGNIFICANT FIBROSIS - so a normal ALT never excludes hepatitis C or advanced disease. SCREEN WITH ANTI-HCV ANTIBODY, and CONFIRM ACTIVE INFECTION WITH HCV RNA BY PCR, because antibody persists after spontaneous or treatment-induced clearance
determine the GENOTYPE where it affects regimen choice. Assess FIBROSIS STAGE non-invasively with TRANSIENT ELASTOGRAPHY (FibroScan), APRI or FIB-4 scores, or by biopsy where necessary

check full blood count for thrombocytopenia, albumin, bilirubin, INR, alpha-fetoprotein, ultrasound, cryoglobulins, rheumatoid factor and complement (low C4) where vasculitis is suspected, and TEST FOR HIV AND HEPATITIS B COINFECTION

redFlags: HEPATITIS C IS NOW CURABLE IN OVER 95% OF CASES WITH 8-12 WEEKS OF ORAL DIRECT-ACTING ANTIVIRAL THERAPY, so the most important action is to IDENTIFY AND REFER EVERY INFECTED PERSON FOR TREATMENT rather than to observe them. Red flags requiring urgent attention: DECOMPENSATED CIRRHOSIS with ascites, jaundice, encephalopathy or VARIceal HAEMORRHAGE presenting as haematemesis and melaena (a medical emergency)
spontaneous bacterial peritonitis

HEPATOCELLULAR CARCINOMA - weight loss, a hard nodular liver, new or refractory ascites, a rising alpha-fetoprotein (ALL PATIENTS WITH CIRRHOSIS REQUIRE 6-MONTHLY ULTRASOUND SURVEILLANCE, AND THIS MUST CONTINUE EVEN AFTER SUCCESSFUL VIRAL CURE, since the cancer risk falls but does not disappear)
severe cryoglobulinaemic vasculitis with progressive renal impairment, purpura, ulceration or neuropathy (needs urgent immunosuppression alongside antiviral therapy)
HIV or HEPATITIS B COINFECTION (screen for HBV before starting DAAs, as HBV REACTIVATION HAS BEEN REPORTED DURING DAA THERAPY)
acute hepatitis C in a healthcare worker after needle-stick exposure (monitor HCV RNA and treat early)
PREGNANCY (DAAs are not currently recommended)
test the infant after 18 months)
renal impairment requiring regimen adjustment
DRUG INTERACTIONS with DAAs, which are extensive and must be checked (amiodarone with sofosbuvir can cause severe bradycardia)
ADVISE COMPLETE ALCOHOL ABSTINENCE, vaccinate against hepatitis A and B, and address injecting-drug harm reduction and reinfection risk

symptoms.sourceText: Hepatitis D occurs only in the presence of hepatitis B, since the delta virus is a defective RNA agent requiring HBsAg as its envelope. coinfection (simultaneous acquisition of HBV and HDV) causes an acute hepatitis with fever, malaise, anorexia, nausea, right upper quadrant pain and jaundice, often biphasic with two peaks of transaminases. superinfection of an existing chronic HBV carrier presents as a severe acute flare or as an unexplained clinical deterioration in previously stable chronic hepatitis B
In superinfection, the rapid appearance of ascites, oedema, jaundice and encephalopathy signalling decompensation
Accelerated progression with cirrhosis developing in 70-80% within 5-10 years, which is far faster than with HBV alone
HDV is the most severe form of viral hepatitis, carrying the highest risk of fulminant hepatitis, the fastest progression to cirrhosis and a 2-6 fold increased risk of hepatocellular carcinoma
Transmission is parenteral and sexual, as for hepatitis B, with injecting drug use, unsafe injections and unscreened blood the main routes
It is endemic in parts of the Mediterranean basin, the Middle East, Central and Northern Asia, West and Central Africa, and the Amazon basin, and vertical transmission is uncommon

signs: Findings mirror those of severe acute or chronic hepatitis B - jaundice, tender hepatomegaly and splenomegaly in the acute phase, with the STIGMATA OF CHRONIC LIVER DISEASE AND PORTAL HYPERTENSION (spider naevi, palmar erythema, clubbing, gynaecomastia, testicular atrophy, a firm irregular or shrunken liver, splenomegaly, ascites, caput medusae, oedema, asterixis and encephalopathy) appearing EARLIER AND PROGRESSING FASTER than in HBV monoinfection. LABORATORY: markedly raised transaminases, often BIPHASIC in coinfection
raised bilirubin

and in advanced disease a falling albumin, rising INR and thrombocytopenia. DIAGNOSIS: SCREEN EVERY HBsAg-POSITIVE PERSON AT LEAST ONCE FOR HDV with TOTAL ANTI-HDV ANTIBODY, and CONFIRM ACTIVE INFECTION WITH HDV RNA BY PCR (anti-HDV IgM indicates active replication)

HDAg can be detected in serum early and in liver tissue. DISTINGUISHING COINFECTION FROM SUPERINFECTION MATTERS FOR PROGNOSIS: in COINFECTION, ANTI-HBc IgM IS POSITIVE (indicating simultaneous acute HBV), the course is usually self-limiting and chronicity is uncommon at under 5%

in SUPERINFECTION, ANTI-HBc IgM IS NEGATIVE while anti-HBc IgG is positive (indicating pre-existing chronic HBV), and CHRONIC HDV INFECTION FOLLOWS IN OVER 90%. Note that HDV typically SUPPRESSES HBV REPLICATION, so the HBV DNA level may be low or undetectable even in severe disease - a low HBV DNA in a deteriorating HBsAg-positive patient should therefore RAISE rather than lower suspicion of delta infection. Stage fibrosis with elastography and monitor alpha-fetoprotein and ultrasound
Febrile symptoms
